transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-03-05
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Laura Chen (Redwood SE), Alex Morgan (Atlas ML), Priya Singh (Platform), Jorge Ramos (Product), Tina Lee (SRE)

Summary:
Quick Optimize walkthrough focusing on batching and caching recommendations for Atlas Retail's conversational product. Covered prefix vs KV caching, batching windows and size, cost model examples, and a plan to run benchmarks on Atlas sample traffic.

Topics:
- Prefix caching for repeated system template and common user prefixes
- KV cache to preserve attention key/value across streams/sessions
- Batching window tradeoffs (latency vs throughput)
- Cost model scenarios and pilot next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir: hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Samir from Redwood, uh I'll kick us off and Laura will do the deep dive on Optimize. Alex, Priya, Jorge, Tina - thanks for making time.
[00:18] Alex: yep thanks Samir, excited to see how we can bring down token cost without hurting p50.
[00:24] Laura: cool, I'll share my screen — just a heads up i've got the Optimize slides and a simple cost model spreadsheet. let me know if you want the sheet after.
[00:34] Priya: yes please, also quick context: most of our workload is a shopping assistant, prompts have a standard system preamble + product context and recent convo history. seq lengths vary a lot — 50 to 800 tokens.
[00:48] Laura: perfect, that's the pattern we normally recommend prefix caching for. so first, prefix vs KV cache — quick def: prefix cache stores repeated prompt prefixes (system messages, templates) and lets the runtime avoid re-encoding that each request; KV cache retains the model's key/value cache across tokens to avoid recomputing attention state across continuation tokens.
[01:12] Jorge: can you say that again — kv cache is like saving the attention memory?
[01:15] Laura: exactly, it's the attention key/values. when you stream continuations within the same session we can reuse the KV cache so only new tokens are computed. for multi-turn with the same context it's huge.
[01:27] Tina: is there persistence across requests or only within a single websocket?
[01:31] Samir: good Q — we support both ephemeral KV (in-memory during a session) and managed KV cache where you can persist keys for a short TTL for reuse across requests. the managed KV option is what we call "shared KV" in the slides — TTL configurable.
[01:45] Alex: got it. any rough numbers on savings?
[01:49] Laura: yes — these are example numbers and i emphasized it's workload dependent: for prompts with a 400-token prefix repeated in 70% of requests, prefix caching can reduce compute per request by ~30-45%. KV cache for multi-turn flows (where you avoid re-attending to 1k tokens) can reduce cost by up to 60-80% on the continuation steps.
[02:12] Alex: that's significant. If we persist KV with TTL, what's the memory overhead and eviction policy?
[02:18] Laura: memory overhead is roughly proportional to sequence length * hidden_size * 2 (keys + values), so we give per-model guidance in the console. eviction is LRU by default and you can set TTL, max entries per customer, and memory caps on Dedicated.
[02:32] Priya: ok, what about correctness? we have concerns about long-lived KV interacting with updated system prompts or user privacy.
[02:39] Samir: super important — we recommend invalidating KV on major context changes (like system prompt updates), and we provide hooks to purge cache on user logout / PII event. also audit logs show cache usage if you need to demonstrate compliance.
[02:55] Jorge: can we auto-invalidate based on probability of prompt drift? like if the system prompt changed recently?
[03:00] Laura: you can tie invalidation to a version id in the request or bump a prefix hash; Optimize can suggest a prefix-hash strategy and the console will show when cached entries are stale.
[03:12] Alex: now batching — what's the recommended window? our SLA is 150ms p50 for chat.
[03:18] Laura: for low-latency interactive chat, we typically recommend micro-batching with a very short window: 5-20ms depending on QPS and tolerance. this gives a 10-30% token cost reduction without noticeably affecting p50. if you can accept a 50-100ms window you get larger batching gains. the console has an estimator that simulates tail latency vs cost.
[03:38] Tina: Our traffic is spiky around promotions — will batching add latency spikes?
[03:42] Samir: batching helps under sustained throughput; under spikes the estimator and routing policies will let you burst to unbatched pools or Dedicated nodes to keep latency bounded. also, Optimize suggests dynamic windows — smaller during low load, slightly larger during steady load.
[03:58] Priya: what's the best batch size?
[04:01] Laura: batch size is less prescriptive than window. with GPUs we often see optimal batch sizes in the 8-64 range for generation, but it's model and seq-length dependent. Optimize's autotuner recommends a pairing: given your seq length distribution it will pick a batch size and window to hit your target SLO while minimizing cost.
[04:20] Alex: show us the cost model example please.
[04:23] Laura: sure — shared screen: this sheet compares three scenarios: (A) hosted default (no KV/prefix caching, 10ms micro-batch), (B) hosted + prefix cache enabled, (C) dedicated + prefix + persisted KV + larger batch window.
[04:36] Laura: for Atlas traffic sample — using our assumptions — scenario B cuts token compute by ~35% vs A, scenario C reduces per-token cost ~55% but includes reserved capacity commit. notice tradeoffs: dedicated has lower unit cost but higher fixed commit.
[04:51] Jorge: what about model variants — lower precision quantization?
[04:55] Laura: yes we also recommend quantized variants for some workload. Optimize suggests fp16 or int8 for non-critical quality flows. Our quality monitoring ties to prompt-evals so if you have critical prompts we run a regression check before recommending quantization.
[05:08] Alex: for our assistant, correctness on slot-filling and safety is key. We can't have hallucination regressions.
[05:13] Samir: totally — part of the pilot is a small eval set we'll run to compare output quality at fp16/int8 vs fp32. Laura will include that in benchmark plan.
[05:22] Laura: i'll note here — we'll run the eval on your test prompts, compare rouge/bleu-ish metrics and manual spot checks.
[05:30] Priya: any pitfalls with prefix caching? 
[05:33] Laura: main pitfall is over-caching changing content — e.g., product catalog snippets in prefix. for that we recommend moving dynamic content into the body and keep truly static instructions as prefix. also watch per-customer memory limits and set TTLs.
[05:47] Tina: how do we instrument savings in our app to verify cost reduction?
[05:52] Samir: Console has token-level cost breakdown and a per-route dashboard; we can also export the raw ledger. Optimize will show before/after delta for cost and latency given sample traffic. We'll provide an attribution report for the pilot.
[06:06] Alex: latency numbers during the demo looked optimistic — are those synthetic?
[06:10] Laura: they are simulated from our runtime model plus some pilot measurements. that's why we want to run a short benchmark with real traffic. in practice we see small variance, but we need your traces for accurate numbers.
[06:22] Jorge: ok timeline — what does a pilot look like?
[06:26] Samir: typical pilot: 2 weeks sandbox benchmark (we run in hosted or in your dedicated test cluster), run three model configs, Optimize autotune batching parameters, run evals, produce cost/latency/quality report, then decide on Dedicated commit or Hosted config.
[06:40] Laura: add-on: if you want, we can also run a small canary in Dedicated for a weekend to validate at scale.
[06:47] Priya: about security — we need SOC2 and KMS details.
[06:50] Samir: we will send the security pack (SOC 2 report, ISO, and KMS/HSM integration docs). we also have VPC options if you go Private.
[06:58] Tina: audit logs for KV access?
[07:00] Laura: yes audit logs include cache hits/misses and who initiated purge operations; logs link to request IDs.
[07:07] Alex: how do we pass KV handles in the API? is it a token or reference?
[07:12] Laura: the API returns a cache-id on store; you then include cache_id in subsequent calls or use our SDK which handles it for you. small transcription here — sometimes the SDK returns it as "kv_ref" or simple header.
[07:25] Jorge: any gotchas integrating into our Node-based lambda infra?
[07:29] Laura: not really — our SDKs are for Node/Python/Go. for lambda we recommend a warmed pool or use the console's warm routing to avoid cold decode latencies.
[07:40] Alex: cost assumptions — can you restate the math you used in the spreadsheet?
[07:43] Laura: sure. base compute cost = model_unit_price * total_decode_tokens. prefix savings subtracts re-encoding cost for prefix tokens, KV savings subtracts attended tokens for continuations. batching reduces per-request overhead by amortizing kernel launch and IO across tokens. the sheet shows per-model unit_price and then multiplication by token counts per scenario.
[08:03] Alex: will you share that sheet with the formulas?
[08:05] Samir: yes we'll share the sheet.
[08:07] Tina: do we need to sign an NDA to share traces?
[08:10] Samir: if you prefer we can work under our standard data processing agreement; we can also accept a sanitized sample. Laura: from a benchmarking standpoint we like raw traces but sanitized is often sufficient.
[08:22] Priya: any recommendations for immediate wins we can implement ourselves before the pilot?
[08:26] Laura: yep — 1) move static instructions to prefix, 2) enable prefix cache on routes with repeated templates, 3) set small batching window (10ms) for interactive end points and monitor p50, 4) add an eval harness for your critical prompts.
[08:41] Alex: that's helpful. Jorge: ok let's recap next steps.
[08:45] Samir: recap — Samir share deck and cost sheet, Laura run benchmark once we get sample, Atlas share 48h traces, follow-up call week of 3/10.
[08:56] Jorge: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[09:00] Samir: thanks all, we'll send notes and action items.

End of meeting.

Notes on transcription quality: occasional mis-hears: "K-V cash" vs KV cache, some speaker label jitter between Samir/Laura on short interjections. timestamps are approximate every 15-60s to mimic Fireflies output.
